The project team also identified the following cross-cutting general themes, considerations, and lessons learned from the project overall: • Simpler Can Be Better: Users should first carefully consider the reasons an ML solution may be necessary and the right approach for a particular challenge. Users should also consider if a simpler approach is suitable before electing to use a more complex ML model. • The Importance of Problem Definition: For developing solutions using ML approaches, it is important to take time to first clearly articulate and define the problem that needs to be solved. Users need to make sure they are solving the right problem. Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs xxvii • The Art of Outlier Removal: Correctly identifying and removing outliers from datasets can be challenging. Users need to negotiate the tension between capturing the 5% edge/extreme data points versus justifying their removal as outliers. • Experimental Design and Collecting Wide-Ranging Data: In developing experimental designs to collect data for ML solutions, users should consider when and where to collect samples so that one captures “interesting” data. In particular, it is important to collect wide-ranging data that describes the system fully and catches any anomalies/perturbations that may take place. Getting wide ranging data near failure points may be difficult to justify for full-scale systems and warrants considering pilot-scale studies that push treatment trains and allow for perturbation and "interesting" data to be collected safely. It is important to determine where to draw the line in data collection such that a sufficient amount of data is collected but not too much such that resources are expended unnecessarily. • Mechanistic Models: For wastewater process challenges, users may want to consider the balance between using a complex mechanistic model versus a simple, black box ML model. • Computer Scientists & the Water Sector: In order to implement ML solutions at WRRFs more widely in the future, the water sector needs to consider how to attract more computer scientists, data scientists, statisticians, etc. Alternatively, the water sector can work to train wastewater process engineers in these disciplines. • Operator Engagement & Training: Operators trust in ML was found to directly correlate to their (1) general understanding of control systems, (2) historical and regular engagement with the engineering team as control upgrades are made, and (3) trust in the process rather than trust in an individual
